moments.title: What the video will cover
moments.text: The presenter introduces functions, input and output variables, notation and types of model.

moments.title: Input and output
moments.text: A function relates an allowed input to an output; the independent variable supplies the input.

moments.title: A child's height over time
moments.text: The example assumes a child is 50 cm at birth and 200 cm at age 15 to build a simple model.

moments.title: Choose variables and axes
moments.text: Age is the input and height is the output. The function notation $H(a)$ represents height at age $a$.

moments.title: A linear model
moments.text: The presenter sketches a straight-line model from 50 cm at birth to 200 cm at age 15 and notes that real growth may not be linear.

moments.title: Form the function
moments.text: The assumed rate is 150 cm over 15 years, or 10 cm per year, giving $H(a)=10a+50$.

moments.title: Evaluate a function
moments.text: Substituting $a=10$ gives $H(10)=150$ cm in the model.

moments.title: Types of functions
moments.text: The presenter briefly surveys linear, quadratic, exponential, logarithmic, sinusoidal and logistic models.

moments.title: A piecewise model
moments.text: To represent a change after age 15, the presenter suggests joining a linear growth rule to a constant-height rule.

notes.title: Function and model
notes.text: The child-height line is an illustrative assumption. The presenter notes that real growth can vary.
notes.write: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. A model should be interpreted only over a suitable domain.

moments.title: The general sine model
moments.text: Introduce $y=a\sin(b(x-c))+d$ and the roles of the parameters.

moments.title: Amplitude
moments.text: An amplitude of $3$ gives a distance of $3$ from the midline to either extreme; it is half the range width.

moments.title: Midline and vertical shift
moments.text: The vertical shift is $4$, so the midline is $y=4$ and the extreme values are $7$ and $1$.

moments.title: Period
moments.text: With $b=2$, the period is $2\pi/2=\pi$ radians of input.

moments.title: Mark quarter-period intervals
moments.text: Divide one period into four equal intervals to locate successive maximum, midline and minimum positions.

moments.title: Account for the horizontal shift
moments.text: The expression $(x-\pi/4)$ shifts the reference sine curve right by $\pi/4$.

moments.title: Plot the shifted sine points
moments.text: Starting from the rising midline crossing at $x=\pi/4$, locate the maximum and subsequent points a quarter-period apart.

moments.title: Complete the smooth curve
moments.text: Connect the points smoothly and extend the cycle over the displayed interval.

moments.title: Summarise the four parameters
moments.text: Review amplitude, midline, period and horizontal shift in the example.

notes.title: A sine graph has no universal starting point
notes.text: The video uses a convenient reference point for one cycle. A sinusoid continues in both directions unless the context or domain restricts it.
notes.write: For this example the graph crosses its midline rising at $x=\pi/4$ and again one period later.

notes.title: Period and amplitude are nonnegative
notes.text: For $a\sin(b(x-c))+d$, use amplitude $|a|$ and period $2\pi/|b|$ when $b\ne0$ and the angle is in radians.
notes.write: A negative $a$ reflects the curve vertically about its midline.

ican.text: I can choose a standard function whose behaviour is consistent with a situation.
I can construct and interpret linear, quadratic, exponential and periodic models.
I can use a model to predict values or solve for an input and assess whether the answer is meaningful.
I can explain how assumptions, domain and extrapolation limit a model.

ku.text: A model represents a relationship using assumptions. Define the variables, units and meaningful domain before interpreting its predictions.
For equal input steps, a linear model $y=mx+c$ has a constant additive change. The slope $m$ is the change in output per unit of input.
A quadratic model $y=ax^2+bx+c$ has a parabolic graph. Its vertex gives a maximum when $a<0$ or a minimum when $a>0$, subject to the model’s domain.
An exponential model $y=A b^t$, with $b>0$, changes by the same factor per unit of $t$. For a rate $r$ per time unit, $b=1+r$ for growth and $b=1-r$ for decay.
A sinusoidal model can represent repeated cycles. Its midline is halfway between maximum and minimum, its amplitude is half their difference, and its period is the input length of a full cycle.
A close fit to observed data alone does not prove that the relationship or its assumptions will remain valid outside the data range. Interpolation and extrapolation have different levels of support.
Check the meaning of a solution: time may be restricted, counts may need whole numbers and a periodic height or temperature can be reached more than once.

misc.weak: A 6% increase means add 6 each year.
misc.better: Multiply the current value by $1.06$ each year. Repeated percentage growth is multiplicative.

misc.weak: An exponential factor of $0.8$ is an 80% decrease.
misc.better: The value retains 80% each period, so it decreases by 20%.

misc.weak: The best-looking fit must predict accurately forever.
misc.better: Check the context, residual pattern, observation range and assumptions, especially when extrapolating.

misc.weak: The maximum is the amplitude of the sinusoid.
misc.better: Amplitude is half the difference between maximum and minimum, measured from the midline.

terms.text: A fixed value in a model whose size determines a feature such as initial value, rate or amplitude.
Using a model to estimate within the range of the observed inputs.
Using a model beyond the observed input range, where the assumptions may be less reliable.
The input interval over which a repeating function completes one cycle.

worked.prompt: A water tank contains $800$ litres at the start of an experiment. A model assumes that it loses 15% of its current volume each hour for the first 6 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Define a model for the volume $V$ after $t$ hours and state its contextual domain.
parts.a: Each hour the tank retains $100\%-15\%=85\%$ of its current volume. Thus $V(t)=800(0.85)^t$ litres for $0\leq t\leq6$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Estimate when the volume first reaches 400 litres.
parts.a: Solve $800(0.85)^t=400$. Then $t=\frac{\ln(0.5)}{\ln(0.85)}\approx4.27$ hours, which lies within the model’s stated domain.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Explain why predicting the volume after 20 hours needs caution.
parts.a: Twenty hours is outside the stated six-hour interval. The constant percentage-loss assumption may cease to hold, for example if the leak rate changes with water level.

kq.q: How can equal increases be distinguished from equal percentage increases?
kq.model: Compare equal input intervals: constant differences suggest a linear relationship, while constant ratios suggest an exponential one.

kq.q: Why should a model’s domain be stated?
kq.model: The expression may produce values outside the period or situation for which the assumptions make sense.

kq.q: How do maximum and minimum determine a sinusoid’s amplitude?
kq.model: Subtract the minimum from the maximum and divide by two. Their average gives the midline.
